Key facts relevant to your FTUE-trigger change:

1\. **Unlock sequences are gated on content reaching the "window"** (item 1–2): an unlock sequence *starts* only when the player scrolls the relevant content into the window — it's not automatic on level-up. The pending state persists across app restarts until the content is seen.

2\. **A sequence is "marked seen" when dismissed** (item 10): FTUE sequences (which include board unlocks like the M board) are marked seen when the player taps "Tap anywhere to continue." So there's a well-defined "sequence is over / seen" moment.

Confirmed: **3rd board = L board**. So the Recommended FTUE trigger is: *the L board's unlock sequence is over + the player starts a new game.*

That mapping has a consequence I need to fold into the draft's wording, and it's worth surfacing now because it's exactly the kind of "sequence is over" ambiguity that would otherwise reach dev unresolved:

Per MD-3620, the **L board is an L/XL/XXL-type unlock** (item 7 + item 10.2), not an M-board/FTUE-type. That means:
- It has **no "Tap anywhere to continue"** step and no darkening.
- It is **marked seen once its unlock sequence has played** — there's no player dismissal.
- It's also **followed by a Booster Reveal animation** (item 7.2), and taps are ignored during the sequence *and* the gap before that reveal (item 11).

So "the L board unlock sequence is over" has a precise meaning I can anchor to MD-3620's own "marked seen" definition — and I should be careful whether "over" means (a) the moment the L-board unlock sequence itself is marked seen, or (b) after the *following* Booster Reveal too. > These conventions surfaced as Erez's feedback during the 2026-07-15 session that split the MD-3676 (Wheels – Recommended) epic into child stories. They apply to content we author (Jira/Notion tickets). Capture them here to decide, in a later session, how to enforce each — a project `CLAUDE.md` formatting rule, a `/content-review` checklist item, or a skill step. None applied yet. The project `CLAUDE.md` already has a FORMATTING section; several of these may extend it.
>
> **Conventions**
> 1. No section heading may repeat the ticket's own title. A ticket named "…- Composition" must not contain a "Composition" heading. Name the section for its content ("Badge placement").
> 2. Sentences, including list items that are full sentences, start with a capital letter.
> 3. Minimum words: cut every word that does not help a reader understand or verify.
> 4. Do not restate context the reader already has. Skip the epic's topic, the screen the feature lives on, and the parent relation (Jira shows the parent link; "Part of MD-XXXX" duplicates it). Drop preamble lines that only re-announce the ticket's subject.
> 5. Do not pad a term or heading with a redundant qualifier ("Behavioural logic" → "Logic"; an acronym the team uses needs no gloss — "FTUE", not "first-time tutorial (FTUE)").
> 6. Use the team's own vocabulary; do not coin terms. Take wording from existing tickets/docs ("UI", not "Presentation"; avoid invented labels like "everyday badge display" or "gender gating").
> 7. List structure must match its lead-in. If a line says "when both are true:", only the two conditions belong under it; a third, separate point goes as its own item, not a sub-bullet. Don't leave two numbered lists stacked with no heading explaining the split.
> 8. Reference approved content, don't restate it. When a ticket covers material approved elsewhere (e.g. Tomer's art), move it verbatim or reference it — never paraphrase approved copy, which can silently change approved meaning.
>
> **Related:** GEN-434 (redline is the default apply mode for staged edits — same session, filed separately).

**Piece 3 — when/where the recommendation is computed (a real architecture decision, and the one I can't settle from the design docs).**
Prod computes server-side at game-end + prepare-for-game and sends fixed values. But Piece 2 requires the badge to respond *live* as the player spins Cards/Helpers on the screen. That's only possible two ways, and this is a genuine choice for dev:

## Why the guard can't vet most claims itself — and what it *can* do

1. **For a narrow slice of claims, you're right — it can vet them, and we should add that.** A claim like "GEN-441 is still open" is machine-checkable: a script can pull the ticket number out of the sentence, ask the tracker for the real status (the project already has a working scripted lookup for exactly this), and compare. That covers the single most common stale-state slip (7 of the 14 logged Class-B cases are exactly this shape). I'd fold it into the guard when the Class-B patterns get built — it's already planned scope, not a new project.
2\. **For everything else, no — because vetting isn't pattern-matching.** The guard is a dumb, instant checklist: "does this sentence look like a factual claim, with no evidence next to it?" But checking whether "this approach can't work" or "the file was deleted" is *true* means opening the right sources, understanding what the claim refers to in this conversation, and judging — that takes an intelligence, not a script.
3\. **Could the guard summon another AI to do that checking at display time? Technically yes, practically no.** A real verification takes tens of seconds to minutes per message; the display guard can't hold the message back meanwhile, so the verdict would land long after you'd read the text. It would also cost a full AI run on every message, the checker would know nothing about our conversation (so it would misjudge what claims even mean), and it can only alter your *screen* — the conversation record would keep the wrong text, creating a confusing split between what you read and what I think I said.
4\. **The design already sends flagged claims to the one agent that** ***can*** **vet them — me, in-session.** The guard's nudge quotes the claim and orders: verify it against the source now, or restate it as unverified. In the soft version I proposed, that lands at the start of my next turn — meaning the vetting waits for your next message.
5\. **The upgrade that matches your question almost exactly is "block mode"** (it was Phase 2 of the original GEN-450 design, deferred): the guard refuses to let me finish my turn while flagged claims stand, so I'm forced to go verify them **immediately and automatically, seconds after the message appears** — no action from you. Four honest caveats, all added to the existing probe step:
6\. It forces another *attempt*, not guaranteed honesty — in principle I could reword the claim to dodge the pattern instead of really checking. The already-planned manual spot-checks watch for exactly that, and the tracker-lookup tier in item 1 is immune to it.
7\. There's a built-in ceiling (after 8 consecutive refusals the system force-ends the turn with a warning) — so the worst case is a claim left standing *with a visible warning*, never an endless loop. I'd have the guard give up after 1–2 attempts anyway; one forced revisit captures most of the value.
8\. Each forced revisit costs an extra model turn on every offending message.
9\. Block mode's exact behavior in this environment is unverified — it goes on the same probe list as the display mechanics (including one specific thing to tune: a session wrap-up summary must not get stuck being blocked).

## First — does moving it actually save tokens?

**Yes.** The project `CLAUDE.md` is loaded in full at the start of every Documentation-project session (you can see it injected in my context this very session). Every line in its FORMATTING section is paid for on every turn of every session, whether or not I'm writing a ticket. So a formatting section that's only relevant *when authoring a ticket* is being paid for constantly but used rarely — that's exactly the "always-loaded cost for a sometimes-need" pattern that's worth moving.

## Is there a better home? Yes — and the project already uses it

There's a proven pattern sitting right here: **`hooks/refs/*.md` + an injection hook.** I verified how it works — `inject-jira-refs.js` watches your prompt, and *only when the turn looks like Jira work* (a ticket key like `MD-1234`, the word "jira", or an `atlassian.net` URL) it injects `refs/jira.md` for that one turn. There are already four such ref files (jira, notion, shell, editing), each moved *out* of the always-loaded global `CLAUDE.md` precisely to cut per-session cost. This is the established, working mechanism for "load it only when relevant."

So the better home is: **a `refs/ticket-formatting.md` file, injected by a hook that fires on ticket-authoring cues** — the same cues the Jira hook already uses (MD-key, atlassian.net, "confluence"). When you're writing a ticket, the rules load; when you're not, they cost nothing.

## But — one honest caveat that matters

The ref-injection mechanism has a **known blind spot**, documented in the Jira hook itself (lines 6–8): it fires on `UserPromptSubmit`, so it only sees your *prompt*. **Ticket formatting work that arises mid-turn — without a prompt cue — isn't covered.** And ticket-authoring very often arises mid-turn: I read code, then draft a ticket, all in one turn where your prompt was just "document feature X." In those turns the prompt may carry no `MD-` key or "jira" token, so the hook wouldn't fire, and I'd draft the ticket *without* the formatting rules loaded.

That's the real tradeoff, and it's the same reasoning the review panel and the load-tier rule apply: **a pointer/hook can't guard a "forgot-to-check" failure.** Formatting rules that must shape a draft I produce *while* drafting are most reliably present if they're always-loaded. The refs that were moved out (Jira/Notion/shell gotchas) are different in kind — they're *reactive* (you hit a gotcha when using that tool, and the tool use itself is the reliable cue). Ticket formatting is *generative* — it has to be in mind before I write, with no reliable tool-cue.

## My recommendation

Given your token concern is real but the reliability risk is also real, the proportionate answer is a **split by trigger-reliability, not a wholesale move:**

- **Keep always-loaded (in project `CLAUDE.md`):** nothing extra — actually, the strongest case is to keep the whole FORMATTING section where it is, because every rule in it is generative-at-draft-time.
- **The lower-cost alternative, if you want the savings:** move the FORMATTING section to `refs/ticket-formatting.md`, injected on ticket cues, **and** add the `document-feature` skill (your main ticket-drafting workflow, which *is* a reliable cue) to read it as an explicit step. That closes most of the mid-turn gap — because when you invoke `/document-feature`, the skill itself pulls the rules in, cue or no cue. The residual gap is ad-hoc ticket edits outside that skill.

**Honest bottom line:** the savings are modest (the FORMATTING section is ~8 lines) and the reliability cost is non-trivial (formatting rules that silently don't load when drafting mid-turn produce badly-formatted tickets you'd have to catch manually). I'd **keep it always-loaded** unless the section grows a lot larger — at which point the refs-file + `document-feature`-step approach becomes worth the residual risk. # /suggest — form the smallest proposal that meets every goal

A single checklist for **forming** a non-routine recommendation before it reaches Erez.
Its whole point is to catch over-engineering and missing alternatives **at formation
time** — before a proposal exists in a shape you have already anchored on, and before a
`/check` review round is spent. `/suggest` **forms**; `/check` **reviews** the formed
proposal independently. They are two stages, not duplicates.

off to `/check` per the existing global-CLAUDE.md "run /check before presenting" bridge.

## When this applies

- A non-routine recommendation, design, architecture, trade-off, or course-of-action call
  you are about to present — whether Erez asked a question or you are proposing unprompted.
- NOT routine requests, plain factual lookups, or finished mechanical tasks — answer those
  directly (same carve-out as the global rules).

## The checklist

1. **Smallest design first.** Start from the bare list of goals the proposal must meet.
   Build the *minimal* thing that meets every one of them, and add nothing no named goal
   requires. If a part isn't traceable to a stated goal, cut it. (This is the anti-over-
   engineering step — the reason this skill exists.)
2. **At least one real alternative, with trade-offs.** Never present a single answer to a
   design/architectural question as if it were the only option. Give a genuine alternative
   and what each choice costs.
3. **Steelman every option you are *not* recommending.** Before recommending one option
   over others, write down the strongest reason to choose each of the others. If you can't
   find a strong reason for an option, you haven't thought about it hard enough yet — go
   think harder before recommending.
4. **First pass is a draft — rate confidence, re-examine if low.** Treat the first version
   as a draft; rate your confidence internally; if it isn't high, re-examine from scratch
   before presenting. (This discipline is owned by the always-loaded "For any non-routine
   answer … treat the first pass as a draft" rule, which fires on a wider set of answers
   than proposals — this is a pointer to it, not a restatement.)
5. **Verify load-bearing claims before asserting them.** Any capability, number, config
   fact, or claim the proposal rests on must be checked against a live source, not stated
   from memory or a summary. (Owned by the always-loaded "Verify before asserting" rule —
   cited here, not restated, because it fires on far more than proposals.)
6. **Hand off to `/check`.** Once the proposal is formed, run it through `/check` per the
   global rule ("run the /check skill on the proposed answer before presenting it"). The
   self-minimize in step 1 is your first pass; `/check`'s Holistic lens is the independent
   backstop — expect it to re-derive minimality from scratch, and don't treat your own
   step-1 pass as making that redundant.

## What this skill does NOT own

To avoid three drifting homes for the same behavior, this skill **cites** rather than
copies the always-loaded rules whose trigger surface is wider than "forming a proposal":
the draft/confidence rule (step 4), the verify-before-asserting rule (step 5), and the
one-item-at-a-time / plain-terms presentation rule (which governs how *any* item goes to
Erez for approval, not only proposals). Those stay in the global `CLAUDE.md`. This skill
owns only the formation discipline that is specific to building a proposal: steps 1–3.

## Relationship to `/check` (read once)

independent review. This is deliberate layering (self-check then independent check), not
duplication — but if either wording is ever edited, update both so they keep describing the
same test.

The bug: I sometimes send you the "📌 For you" summary twice in a row in the same turn. It's rare — twice in the last three weeks — but five shipped fixes haven't killed it. Going through the full record, four things explain why:

1\. **Every fix attacked the symptom, downstream of the cause.** The duplicates start when one of two automatic end-of-turn checkers injects a reminder note *after* my block already went out — that note is what makes me write a second block. Every fix so far left those reminders firing and tried to catch or block the duplicate afterward. That requires a pattern-match on my own formatting, which varies (26% of real blocks used formats the catcher couldn't see), and the "blocking" arm can't un-show a message already on your screen — its one real-life firing produced a *third* copy instead.

2\. **The repair grew far bigger than the problem.** The last attempt was two rewritten checkers, one brand-new checker, a settings change, a scan procedure, and a ten-script measuring kit. At that size, every fix round measurably introduced at least one new bug — three rounds in a row — and most of the bugs were in the measuring kit, not the fix. Review can't converge on an object that big; each round's fixes feed the next round's findings.

3\. **Our "verified" signals weren't attached to the failure surface.** The "53/53 tests pass" came from a suite that never loads the files that were broken; two measuring scripts reported all-clear while silently broken; and the scheduled checkup that was supposed to watch the results has silently *vanished* from the task registry — nothing has been watching since Aug 9.

4\. **Three sessions of working on copies without installing** let the copies and the live files drift apart, which manufactured its own class of bugs.

It's not a model-tier issue — both Opus and Fable rounds failed the same way, because the failing dimension was the size and placement of the change, not reviewer strength.

## The proposal (the small re-cut you chose, now fully specified and panel-converged)

The design turns the provocation **off at its two sources** instead of catching the result: each checker now recognizes "the block already went out" (using the already-reviewed wider format-matcher) and **stays completely silent** — no reminder, no follow-up turn, nothing for a duplicate to ride on. The blocker arm that once made a third copy is retired to a log-only sighting. That's it: a few dozen lines edited directly in the two live files, nothing new ships, no settings change, and the measuring kit is out of the approval path entirely (its repairs happen after, as cleanup). If the format-matcher ever misses a new block style, behavior falls back to exactly today's — it cannot make anything worse by missing. The vanished scheduled checkup gets re-created at install and verified, and it watches three tripwires: any new duplicate of the kinds this closes (reopen the design, don't patch), any duplicate of the kind the banked mid-turn detector could catch (that's its un-freeze trigger), and "the suppressors have gone quiet" (recognizer drift).

- The problem is purely the **bad-network tail**: the day your wifi is flaky or you're offline, Option 2 would stall your session start for up to 90 seconds every time, until it times out.

First, the key mechanism difference: in **Option 2**, the session-start hook does the fast local snapshot, then kicks off the GitHub upload as a **background job it does not wait for** — so the hook returns *before knowing whether the upload succeeded*. Here's specifically what gets less precise:

**1. The timer records "attempted," not "succeeded."**
Because the hook doesn't wait for the upload, it can only stamp the timer with "I *started* an upload at 10:00" — it can't stamp "an upload *succeeded* at 10:00." So if that upload silently fails (GitHub hiccup, network blip at that moment), the timer still says "backed up at 10:00," and the next session within 5 minutes gets **skipped** — meaning a failed upload isn't retried for up to 5 minutes. This is *exactly* the bug the reviewers made me fix in Option 1. Option 2 reintroduces it in a milder form.
- **How bad is it, really?** The work is never lost — it's safe on your disk, and the *next* session after the 5-min window uploads the current state (a full snapshot, so it captures everything). So the worst case is a **backup that's up to a few minutes staler than you'd think**, not lost data. On your solid network, the "upload silently failed" case is rare to begin with.

**2. No precise success accounting across your repos.**
Option 1 tracked, per session, exactly which repos pushed / were unchanged / failed transiently / failed durably, and only advanced the timer when everything was genuinely covered. Option 2 doesn't look at that — it fires the upload and moves on. So:
- If one repo uploads fine but another was momentarily unreachable, Option 2 doesn't distinguish — it just stamped "attempted at 10:00" and may skip the next session's retry of the repo that missed. Again: not lost (next window catches it), just potentially a few minutes staler.

**3. The "stuck repo" edge case is handled *better*, not worse, in Option 2.**
This is the flip side. In Option 1, the reviewers found that a permanently-stuck repo (a flagged secret, an oversize file) would make the timer *never* advance → flash *never* suppressed. Option 2 sidesteps that entirely: it doesn't gate the timer on success at all, so a stuck repo doesn't block the throttle. So on *this* edge case, Option 2 is actually cleaner.

**4. Failure visibility is unchanged.**
Both options keep the existing failure queue — a genuinely failed upload still gets logged and surfaced to you next session. Option 2 doesn't lose the "you'll be told if a backup failed" safety net. It only loses the *precision of the retry timing*, not the *awareness*.

|---|---|---|
| Flash gone? | Yes | Yes |

**The core tension:** the template's byte-cursor answers "which records have I *shown*?" — monotonic, append-only-safe. GEN-435 needs richer per-item state: a marker is `pending` → then `survived` (clear it) or `killed` (alert). So there are genuinely different designs for how state is tracked. Breadth pass on the state model:

1. **Byte-cursor only (template as-is):** shows each pending marker once, then advances past it. ✗ Wrong — this resolves on first sight; it can't represent "still pending, check again next time," which is exactly what a survival check needs.
2. **Reader writes resolution back into the queue** (flip a `surfaced`/`resolved` flag in-place). ✗ Violates the append-only-never-write invariant the template's comments call load-bearing; races the writer.
3. **Separate reader-owned *state* file** (not just a byte cursor): the surfacer reads ALL pending markers each session, and keeps its own JSON state `{markerId → {firstSeen, lastChecked, status}}`. Each session it re-checks artifact existence for every not-yet-resolved marker; clears (marks resolved in its own state) on survival, alerts on kill. The queue stays strictly append-only; all mutation is in the reader's own file. ✓ This is the append-only-safe way to hold richer-than-cursor state, and it's the natural generalization of the cursor idea.
4. **A minimum-dwell before resolving** (e.g. don't clear until the marker is ≥ N hours/1 session-gap old), so "survived" means "survived real elapsed time," not "existed at the very next startup seconds later." ✓ needed — folds into option 3's state.

**The problem:** The queue file is append-only (the writer never rewrites it, and a background sweep may append at any moment). Each record has `surfaced: false`. To avoid re-showing the same failures every session, the surfacer must record "already shown." Rewriting the file in place to flip `surfaced` to `true` breaks the append-only contract and races the concurrent writer.

Let me think through the options for how the surfacer tracks what it has already shown, since this is the foundational primitive:

**Option A — rewrite the queue file in place**, flipping `surfaced: false → true`. Rejected: directly violates the append-only contract the writer depends on, and races a concurrent sweep append (could truncate a line the sweep just wrote, or lose a sweep append that lands between the surfacer's read and write). This is a corruption risk on the exact file whose integrity the backup system depends on.

**Option B — a separate "high-water mark" cursor file.** The surfacer records how far into the queue it has read (e.g. byte offset or a count of lines consumed), stored in its own small file it fully owns. Next session, it reads only lines past the mark. The queue file itself is never touched — stays truly append-only. No race with the sweep writer. This matches the "read+mark" intent without rewriting the shared file. The `surfaced` field in the record becomes effectively vestigial (or a within-file hint), but the cursor is the real mechanism.

**Option C — the surfacer moves consumed lines to an archive file** (read all, show unsurfaced, append them to `backup-sweep-failures.archive.jsonl`, then truncate the live queue). Rejected: truncating the live queue races the concurrent sweep exactly like Option A.

Sharp question — and the answer depends entirely on *how* A is done. Done naively, **yes, it leaks.** Done correctly, **no.** Let me be precise, because this is exactly the kind of thing worth getting right.

**How it would leak (the naive way):** if I read the sheet cell and print the token to stdout — or set it in one command and inspect it in another — the value lands in a tool *result*, which becomes part of my context and the session transcript. That's a real leak: it'd sit in the transcript, and if this session were ever attached to a feedback report (like the `/feedback` we just discussed), it'd travel. So a naive A is genuinely unsafe.

**How to do A without leaking:** keep the token inside a **single shell invocation**, from read to use, and never emit it. The token flows: secure sheet → a shell variable → the `curl` Authorization header → discarded when the command ends. It's never printed, never returned in a result. The only thing that comes back to my context is curl's *response* (the created comment's URL), not the token. This is exactly how the Notion-token pattern already works — `notion-ticket-lookup.ps1` reads the token from the vault and passes it to curl within one script, and the token never appears in any result. Same discipline.

Concretely, the safeguards:
- Read the sheet and extract the cell, assign to a variable, and reference `$VAR` only inside the `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAR"` — all in **one** Bash call.
- **Never** `echo`/`Write-Output` the variable; never `curl -v` (logs headers); print only curl's JSON response piped through a filter that extracts just the comment URL.
- The command *string itself* gets logged to `deferred-calls.jsonl`, but it contains `$VAR`, not the literal token — and that log is redacted for token-shaped strings anyway.

**But there's a residual risk even done right, and I should name it:** the *command text* I write will be visible in my context and the transcript (that's unavoidable — I author it). As long as it references the variable and never the literal value, the secret itself doesn't appear. The failure mode is if the sheet-read step accidentally surfaces the value (e.g., the extraction prints the whole row). I'd guard that by extracting precisely and routing only the non-secret output back.

Reading it might go through the Google Drive MCP tools, whose **results return to my context** — if that tool returns the cell value, the token *is* in a tool result, leaked, regardless of my shell hygiene. That's the part I can't fully guarantee is leak-proof, because I don't control what the Drive tool echoes back. That's a real strike against A.

## Proposal (formed via `/suggest`; **not yet reviewed** — `/check` + `/vet-rule` come next)

**The core insight:** your two complaints have *different* root causes and need *different* fixes. Lumping them is why prior attempts stalled.

**Failure 1 — missing tags — is an enforcement gap.** It's fixable with a hook, and GEN-466's "no hook possible" conclusion doesn't apply: that was about reading the live effort *value* at prompt-time; this only needs end-of-turn *string detection* of whether a block with a decision path is missing its `(effort, model)` tag. The existing `stop-foryou-nudge.js` already proves this exact pattern works. **Fix: extend the Stop-hook enforcement** so that when a "📌 For you" block contains a proposed path but no `(…, …)` tag, it nudges — same mechanism that already keeps the block itself reliable.

**Failure 2 — fabricated numbers — is a grounding gap**, and *cannot* be fixed by a hook (a hook can't tell whether the number is right). The leverage here is to **remove the separate lookup**: the fabrication happens largely because the grounding lives in `effort-model-reference.md`, a file nothing forces me to open, so I produce a plausible number from intuition instead. Fix: **inline the stable mapping into the rule text itself** (the 4-row work-type→effort table is small and model-independent), so the grounding is right there at the point of use. The reference file stays as the deeper/numeric backup, but the everyday lookup is inline. This keeps the tag **terse** (your option 2) — the inlining is in the *rule*, not in the output.

**What I'd keep unchanged:** the bare output format (`high, Opus 4.8`, no rationale) — that's your locked decision, and option 2 preserves it.

**The honest residual (check 8):** the grounding fix is still ultimately self-policed — inlining the table makes the right answer *easy and adjacent*, but nothing can *force* me to consult it or *verify* the number is correct, because only I know the work-type. It reduces fabrication by removing the friction that causes it; it doesn't eliminate the possibility. The reliability fix (hook) is genuinely enforced. So: **one half becomes enforced, the other half becomes low-friction-but-still-trusted.** I won't oversell it as airtight.

**Alternative I considered and rejected (check 5/6):** requiring me to *cite the reference row* in the output (option d) — this would make grounding visible/checkable by you. Its strength: you could catch a wrong lookup. Why I don't recommend it: it breaks the terse format you locked, adding a rationale clause to every tag — exactly what you said you didn't want. Inlining (f) gets most of the grounding benefit without touching the output. If you'd rather trade terseness for verifiability, (d) is the one to pick — your call.

**Can a sub-agent solve the anchoring problem? Partly — but there's a hard mechanical wall.**

What a sub-agent *does* give you: genuine cold context. A spawned agent gets **only the prompt you hand it** — it cannot see the first pass's findings, the fixes, or the conversation. That's real, true blindness — exactly the independence the same-session second pass lacks. On that axis, yes, a sub-agent solves it.

But here's the wall, confirmed from the two things I just checked:
- The only defined agent (`check-reviewer`) is **read-only: `Read, Grep, Glob, ToolSearch, WebSearch, WebFetch`** — no shell, no ability to run `/code-review`, and it can't apply fixes.
- The general-purpose agent (`claude`, tools `*`) *could* in principle run tools, but the global rule I'm operating under states plainly: **sub-agents can't run Bash/PowerShell here — shell calls are denied outright** (they run non-interactively and can't surface a permission prompt). And `/code-review` reviews the live working tree via git/shell.

So a sub-agent can be a **cold reviewer**, but it cannot be a cold **`/code-review` run**. It would be reading the diff with Read/Grep/Glob and reasoning — a capable static review, but not the same tool the first pass used, and it can't do the live-probe things (`node --check`, planting a token) that caught the actual GEN-382 fail-opens.

That gives us a clear option space:

**Option 1 — Second pass as a cold sub-agent reviewer (static).** Spawn a fresh agent, hand it only the diff + the adversarial brief, get findings back, you apply fixes in the main session. **Gains:** true context independence — the anchoring weakness is genuinely gone. **Costs:** it's a static diff read, not a `/code-review` invocation and not live-fire; and it's more orchestration wiring in the skill (spawn, collect, merge, apply). Net: trades a *stronger* review mechanism (real `/code-review` + live-verify) for *stronger independence*. Given that Step 4 (live-verify) already exercises the runtime separately, the lost live-probe isn't fully lost — but the second pass is weaker as a *review*.

**Option 2 — The one I'd actually reach for: a fresh, separate session.** The cleanest way to get a genuinely cold second `/code-review` — full tool access, real live working tree, real `node --check`, *and* zero context bleed — is to run it in a **new session** (or after `/clear`), pointed at the same working copy. This is precisely how GEN-414 was *discovered*: the killer second pass wasn't a sub-agent, it was literally **the next session** re-reviewing the same script cold. That's the strongest possible independence and keeps the full `/code-review` power. **Cost:** it's not a single unbroken `/vet-code` run — the flow pauses, you start a fresh session to do pass 2, then resume. More friction, and it breaks the "one skill, start to finish" shape.

**Option 3 — Keep same-session + adversarial brief (the converged design).** Weakest independence, but full `/code-review` power, live-fire intact, zero orchestration cost, and empirically it *did* catch the bugs.

A sub-agent buys the independence but *pays for it by downgrading the review to a static read*; a fresh session buys the same independence with **no downgrade** — you keep real `/code-review` and live-verify. The **classifier** here is Claude Code's **auto-mode permission classifier** — a safety check that runs *before* certain tool calls to decide whether they're safe to auto-approve, block, or route to you for a prompt. It's the thing that produced those "temporarily unavailable" / "Stage 2 classifier error" messages.

Here's the fuller picture:

**What it is.** When Claude Code runs in "auto" permission mode, not every tool call I make is waved through automatically. For calls that aren't obviously read-only-and-safe (running a shell command that changes state, writing outside the working directory, etc.), the harness sends the proposed action to a **separate, server-side classifier model** whose only job is to judge: is this safe to allow, should it be blocked, or should the user be asked? It's a distinct model from the one I'm running on (Opus 4.8) — you don't pick it with `/model`; Anthropic configures it on the server.

**Why it exists.** It's a guardrail so that in auto mode, risky actions get gated without you having to approve every single call by hand. It's a different layer from the `auto-approve.js` *hook* (your own local rules, like the chain-guard that blocked `cd && git push`). The hook is your custom policy; the classifier is Anthropic's built-in safety model. A call can be stopped by either.

**What "fails closed" means.** When the classifier model itself is momentarily unreachable or overloaded (which is what "claude-opus-4-8 is temporarily unavailable" / "Stage 2 classifier error" signals), it can't return a safe/unsafe verdict. Rather than guess and risk allowing something dangerous, the system **refuses the call** — it errs on the side of blocking. That's "failing closed": when unsure, deny rather than allow. That's why the block message says "usually transient — retrying often succeeds": once the model is reachable again a moment later, the identical call gets a real verdict and goes through.

**Why this isn't a real denial.** A genuine denial is a *decision* — "this action is unsafe, no." That's deterministic: retry it and it fails again. What happened twice this turn (the git push, the marker write) was the classifier being temporarily *unavailable to decide at all* — proven by the identical retry succeeding within seconds. Availability failure, not judgment. That's the distinction we worked out and recorded on GEN-394, and it's why neither counts as the GEN-316 case (which is specifically the classifier *wrongly deciding* to deny a call it should have allowed).

Short version: it's an Anthropic-run safety model that pre-screens risky tool calls in auto mode; when it's briefly down it blocks-by-default, and a retry a second later normally clears it.

**Title:** Prevent the `HISTORY.md` table of contents from drifting out of sync with the entries

**Parent:** GEN-86 (Improve AI Infra epic)

**Body:**

## Problem
The wrap-up procedure (`/wrap`, Step 4) requires two coordinated writes to a project's `HISTORY.md`: prepend the new dated entry to the body, **and** prepend a matching one-line entry to the `## Table of contents`. These are done by hand, as two separate edits, with nothing verifying they stay in sync. When the TOC write is skipped or the numbering is wrong, the file silently drifts — the body and TOC disagree — and it isn't caught until someone reads the file closely.

## Evidence (2026-07-15, Improve AI Infra)
Multiple failures surfaced in a single day on `Improve AI Infra/HISTORY.md`:
1. **Missing TOC line (single-session):** a wrap prepended the `(4)` body entry but never added its TOC line.
2. **Wrong numbering (single-session):** the same wrap labelled its entry `(3)` when a `(3)` already existed that day (correct was `(4)`) — because the author read only the file's first ~60 lines (a preview that cut off before the TOC header at line 16) and generalized "no TOC exists" from that partial read.
3. **Body/TOC inversion (older gap):** an earlier session ("Backup-sweep PowerShell auto-open/close") wrote its full summary into the *TOC* slot and never created a body entry at all.
4. **Missing TOC line (concurrency):** a concurrent session ("For you block rules") committed a `(5)` body entry with no TOC line — a consequence of the concurrent-write race tracked in GEN-218.

All four were reconciled by hand this session. Points 1–2 also produced a GEN-58 Class-A reasoning-failure entry (asserting a file's structure from a partial read).

## Why prose alone isn't enough
Step 4 already *says* to maintain the TOC. It drifted anyway, because it depends on a human remembering to make a second, correctly-ordered edit every time. This is the kind of gotcha better closed by a mechanism than by more instruction.

## Directions to consider (settle during design; run `/check` before building)
- **Generate the TOC from the entries** rather than hand-maintaining it — a script that (re)builds `## Table of contents` from the body's dated headers, run as part of `/wrap`, so the two can't disagree by construction.
- **A validator** (wrap step or hook) that checks body-vs-TOC consistency (same set of dated entries, same order, no duplicate numbers) and fails/flags on mismatch.
- **Sourcing discipline:** the wrap's HISTORY step should read the whole file's entry/TOC structure (or grep for the TOC header) before editing — never infer structure from a truncated read. (Overlaps the GEN-58 Class-A lesson.)

## Boundaries / related
- The concurrency-caused variant (point 4) is **GEN-218's** domain (concurrent sessions overwriting project files); this ticket is about keeping body and TOC internally consistent regardless of cause. Cross-linked, not duplicated.
- Applies to every project's `HISTORY.md`, not just Improve AI Infra.

- On a simple prompt, the model **skips thinking on its own** — docs: adaptive reasoning *"makes thinking optional on each step, so Claude can respond faster to routine prompts."*

With it `false`, you've been forcing thinking *off* everywhere; setting it `true` hands the per-prompt decision to the model — which is exactly the automatic behavior you asked for. The setting you rejected as "default on" is actually "let the model choose per prompt."

Lower effort reduces thinking *and* reasoning depth on tool calls, code, everything — you'd be dialing down capability globally to control one thing. And it doesn't fully deliver "on when needed": at `low`, a genuinely hard prompt gets less than it should. It controls the *average*, not the *per-prompt* decision. The switch-to-allow option gives you the real per-prompt adaptivity; effort-down just lowers the whole baseline.

**The idea in plain terms.** When you change a hook or script today, the system already does this: after the review runs, it writes a little sealed receipt tied to that exact file and its exact contents, and the edit is hard-blocked unless a matching receipt exists — and the moment that unlocks it is a prompt *you* approve. So the fix is to **reuse that same machine for a second kind of edit** (your rules, skills, and CLAUDE.md), with a lighter review bar (one `/check` panel instead of the full code-review-plus-testing gauntlet that code demands).

**On your two skills specifically:**
- **`/vet-code`** — reuse its *mechanism* (the receipt + the you-approve-the-unlock prompt), but **not by bolting onto `/vet-code` itself**. The review panel was firm on this: `/vet-code` is built for code and forces things like two code reviews and antivirus checks that make no sense for a rule edit. Baking rule-enforcement into it would drag rule edits through irrelevant, heavy steps. So it becomes its **own lightweight gate** that borrows the plumbing — not an extension of `/vet-code`.
- **`/suggest`** — stays a checklist I follow, not an enforcement point (it can't block or record anything). Putting "you must run /check" into it is just more of the prose the ticket says already failed. It's the *detector* that routes to `/check`, nothing more.

**What the review panel caught and I've now built in** (these are the difference between a real gate and a fake one):
1. **The receipt must prove a review actually happened** — it references the real reviewer transcripts on disk and the unlock step confirms they exist, so it can't be faked by just writing "review: done" into a file.
2. **You see the verdict when you approve** — the unlock prompt shows you the review outcome and any findings, so your approval is informed, not a blind rubber-stamp.
3. **Typo/formatting fixes get a fast lane, but a machine-checked one** — the "this is just a mechanical fix" label is verified automatically (the change really is whitespace/spelling only); a substantive edit can't sneak through by mislabeling itself.
4. **The global-rules file is caught at the right place** — because your global CLAUDE.md is only ever edited through that gatekeeper script, the gate has to watch the *script path*, not just direct edits (a direct edit is already blocked). Miss this and the gate would've been dead on arrival for your most important file.
5. **Skills live in nested folders** (I verified the live layout) — the matching logic has to account for that or it silently never fires.

**Two-axis priority.** Urgency (my existing three definitions) sets the *floor*; gain÷effort *orders within and can lift one step*.

- **Gain** — estimated on a 1–3 scale: 1 = minor/cosmetic, 2 = meaningful improvement, 3 = large impact (unblocks work, fixes real pain, or high leverage across future work).
- **Effort** — estimated on a 1–3 scale: 1 = quick (<~30 min / one sitting), 2 = moderate (a session), 3 = large (multi-session or uncertain).
- **Ratio** = gain ÷ effort (range 0.33–3). Higher = better return.

**How they combine:** urgency picks the base level (High 🔥 / Medium / Low). Then ratio adjusts *within*: a high ratio (≥2) can bump a ticket up one level; a low ratio (≤0.5) can drop it one. You asked what these Notion approval gates are, since you keep hitting them even on "bypass permissions" — and asked me to verify. I checked your actual hook config, not memory.

**What it is:** a deliberate safety hook you (well, past sessions) built, named `notion-schema-guard.js`, registered in your global `settings.json` as a **PreToolUse** hook. It's not a bug and not Notion's doing — it's your own tooling working as designed.

**Why "bypass permissions" doesn't stop it:** "Bypass permissions" (and auto-approve) control the *normal* permission flow. This hook sits *above* that flow. When it matches a dangerous Notion operation it returns a decision called `ask`, which — per Claude Code's design — **forces an interactive Allow/Deny prompt no matter what permission mode you're in.** That's the whole point: it was built specifically so a risky Notion write can never slip through silently, even under auto/bypass mode. So the gate you're seeing is not a mode being ignored — it's a hook intentionally overriding the mode.

**What it gates (only these — everything else Notion passes silently):**
1\. **Destructive schema changes** — dropping/altering/renaming a database column, or trashing a whole data source.
2\. **Re-parenting writes** — setting an "inverse-of-parent" relation (a property ending `(Parent item)`), which silently moves a page to a new parent. Fires both when editing and when creating a page.
3\. **Raw REST/curl writes to Notion** (`api.notion.com`) — the case in your screenshot. Because a shell command's payload is opaque to the hook (it can't read the body), it **can't tell which risk class the write is, so it asks on *every* Notion write of this kind.** That coarseness is forced, not a mistake — hence you get prompted even for a benign write like the GEN-382 "mark resolved" edit shown.

**Why it feels more frequent lately:** the raw-REST/curl arm (item 3) was added under GEN-378 — recently. Before that, only MCP-tool-based schema/relation writes were gated. Now any curl/Invoke-WebRequest write to Notion trips it too, which is why routine block-edits done via curl now prompt.

**Bottom line:** working as intended; the prompt is your own guardrail, and it's correct that bypass mode doesn't silence it. Ordinary Notion reads and additive edits are *not* gated — only the three destructive/opaque classes above.

**If you want fewer prompts,** the honest options and their trade-offs:
- **Leave it** — safest; you keep the confirm on genuinely dangerous ops but eat prompts on benign curl writes.
- **Route benign edits through the MCP tools instead of curl** — the MCP arms inspect the actual payload, so a benign `notion-update-page` content edit passes silently; only true schema/re-parent writes prompt. This removes most of your recent prompts without weakening the real guard.
- **Narrow the shell arm** — technically possible but risky, since narrowing depends on parsing opaque shell bodies; I'd advise against it.

**Why recent sessions used curl anyway** — two legitimate reasons, so this isn't "always use MCP":
- **Staleness / freshness** — your own project rule says `notion-fetch` reads a *lagging cache*, and for time-sensitive reconciliation you should read via REST directly (always live). That pushed sessions toward the REST/curl path for reads, and writing in the same channel is natural.
- **PS quoting pain** — there's a documented curl-body-to-temp-file workaround, i.e. sessions had already invested in making curl writes work.

Neither reason applies to a simple **write** like "mark block resolved." That's pure MCP territory.

**The honest trade-off of switching to MCP for writes:**
- **Upside:** benign content/property edits stop prompting you entirely. The real guardrail (schema DDL, re-parenting) still fires — through the MCP arms, which are *smarter* because they read the payload.
- **Downside:** MCP writes go through the lagging cache, so for a write that must land on top of the very latest state (racing another editor/UI), curl-to-REST is still the safer channel — and there you *should* keep the prompt.

**My recommendation:** default Notion **writes** to the MCP `notion-update-page` tool; reserve raw REST/curl for reads that must be live, and for writes racing an out-of-band edit. This eliminates most of your recent prompts without weakening the guard at all.

Here's the actual design question: **a raw log is a passive store; something active has to read it and put a number in front of us.** There are a few genuinely different ways to make that happen, and they differ in what you'd have to do:

The honest constraint first: the detection is the *same* fuzzy classifier problem the reviewers flagged for the blocking hook — "did that reply narrate a nudge?" has no clean marker. So whatever surfaces, **the count will be approximate** (some false hits, some misses). That's acceptable for a trend signal ("is this roughly happening a lot, a little, or not at all?") but it is not a precise instrument, and I shouldn't present it as one.

Given that, the surfacing options:

1. **Wrap-time report (my recommended default).** The logger writes events to the file; the `/wrap` end-of-session routine reads the file, counts events since the last wrap, and puts one line in your wrap report: e.g. *"nudge-narration logger: 3 suspected events across 2 sessions since [date]."* You see it every time you end a session — no new habit, no separate place to look. When the number stays high after the reframe ships, that line is your signal to re-evaluate. This is the lightest thing that actually reaches you.

2. **A threshold self-trigger.** The logger (or a small scheduled check) fires a proactive notification *only* when events cross some bar — say, "3+ in a single session" or "still occurring N sessions after the reframe date." Silent until it matters, louder when it does. Costs more to build (needs a threshold, a scheduler, and dedup so it doesn't nag), and a fuzzy classifier driving an alert threshold means occasional false alarms.

3. **On-demand only.** Logger just writes; nothing surfaces unless you or I explicitly go look (e.g. "show me the narration log"). Cheapest to build, but it relies on someone *remembering* to ask — which, given the whole point is catching a slow-recurring problem, is the weakest link. This is close to the rot case.

My recommendation is **option 1**: fold the read into `/wrap`, because it's the one place you reliably already look at end-of-session summaries, so the signal can't sit unseen. If a single line at wrap turns out too passive once we see real numbers, adding the option-2 threshold alert on top is a small follow-on — but I wouldn't build the alerting machinery before we even know the events are frequent enough to warrant it.

One thing this also settles: **the logger needs an explicit "evaluate by" definition baked into what surfaces**, or a count is just a number. Concretely — the reframe ships on date D; the wrap line should read something like *"since D: N suspected narration events"*, so a glance tells you whether it dropped after the change. I'd record that success criterion on GEN-469 when we build it (e.g. "if suspected events don't drop meaningfully within ~5 sessions after D, the reframe didn't hold → revisit the blocking hook").

The skill (if we keep the wording in one) is just the **storage** for the checklist; the hook is the **trigger and enforcer**. The skill never has to be "remembered" — the hook surfaces its content automatically.

So it can't catch the "missing" case (block absent when it should be present) without also firing on every conversational turn, which would force me to bolt an empty block onto pure-chat replies — the exact noise we're trying to avoid.

So a hook lands in a bind: enforce presence *always* → false alarms on conversational turns; enforce presence *never* → no help. The judgment of "was a block warranted here" is inherently mine.

**What actually happens (verified in `Code.js` lines 1113-1132):**

The automation doesn't receive a *message* from the supplier saying anything. It **clicks the download link itself** (`UrlFetchApp.fetch`, line 1115) and reads the **technical response code** the provider's server returns:

- Code **200** = here's the file → downloaded and saved.
- Code **401/403** = login required.
- Code **202** = the server accepted the request but the PDF is still being generated. The code waits 3 seconds, tries **once** more (lines 1123-1126), and if it's *still* 202, marks the link `pending202` (line 1131-1132) — "still being prepared."

So the accurate phrasing isn't "the supplier says it isn't ready." It's: **when the automation tries to download the invoice, the provider's server replies with the technical 'still generating, not ready yet' signal (HTTP 202), twice in a row.** That's the "not-ready link" I referred to. My earlier wording implied a human/email message; it's actually a server response code to an automated download attempt. I was wrong to phrase it that way.

**Why this matters for your original question** (does the not-ready link identify *which* invoice it's for): The `pending202` result at line 1131-1132 carries **only** `pending202: true` and a generic reason string — no filename, no invoice number, no amount. The 202 means the file literally doesn't exist yet on the server, so there's nothing to identify it by. However, the *link itself* still exists in the email — with its clickable anchor text and its web address — and those are captured separately when the link is first read (I confirmed earlier they're stored as `sourceUrl` and `anchorText`). So the identifying detail, **if any exists**, lives in the email's link text/URL, not in the not-ready response.

You said: "pick up gen 642". I did the investigation it asks for, and it comes down to one decision that's yours.

**What the question is.** Today, when a document arrives, the automation first looks at the *file names* already sitting in the target month folder. If it finds one with the same supplier and the same month, it refuses to file the new document and flags it for you — without ever opening either file. That is the check that lost Inbal Peer's genuine July tax invoice for eleven days: her payment request was already on file, the names matched, and the invoice was withheld. Behind that check sit three deeper ones that all decide by actually *reading* the documents.

**What I found.** Every file the name check can catch is also examined by the reading-based check — so nothing would go unchecked if the name check went away. I tested the reading-based check on the hardest real cases in your Drive: your four separate Anthropic invoices from July (different invoice numbers, different amounts — $45, $90, $99.96, $325 — two of them issued the very same day), plus the exact Inbal Peer pair that caused the loss, plus a document against a copy of itself. Five out of five verdicts correct. The name check, meanwhile, currently only looks at 26 of the 258 files in your 2026 expenses folder, because the rest don't carry the label it needs — so it protects far less than it appears to.

**My recommendation: remove the name check, and have the daily summary tell you whenever something was filed next to an existing file for the same supplier and month.** What you gain: genuine documents stop being held back — the Anthropic pattern (several real invoices from one supplier in one month) is exactly what the current check wrongly rejects. What you risk: the reader becomes the only judge for genuine lookalikes, so if it ever wrongly calls two copies of the same document "different", you'd get a second copy filed. Adding the summary note is what makes that visible rather than silent, and it costs nothing — the information is already to hand. Speed is a non-issue: about 5–8 seconds per comparison, no meaningful change to how long a run takes.

**The two alternatives, so you can weigh them:** remove the check *without* the summary note — very slightly simpler, but you'd never be told when a near-duplicate was filed; or leave everything as it is — nothing can slip through, but genuine documents keep getting withheld, which is the failure that has actually happened to you.

**Title:** Stop payment requests being mislabelled as invoices and blocking the real tax invoice from filing

**Properties:** Parent item [GEN-21](https://app.notion.com/p/36a6e495d07c8048beade188b3d376fd) · Type Bug · Project AI · Status In Progress · Assignee unassigned (Claude) · Urgency **Urgent** · Gain ratio **1** · Priority **Highest** (derived: Urgent + Gain 1)

**Body:**

> **The problem.** Muuula's vendors often send a payment request first (an Israeli חשבון עסקה / proforma — not a document the bookkeeper can record or reclaim VAT against), then the genuine tax invoice after payment. The automation has no concept of a payment request: the document-type list in both reader prompts (`Code.js:924`, `Code.js:2193`) is invoice / receipt / invoice_receipt / statement / neither. So on 31 July 2026 Inbal Peer's `ProformaInvoice_90028.pdf` was filed as `Inbal Peer August 2026 invoice.pdf`.
>
> **The damage, already done.** The check at `Code.js:2620-2628` refuses to file a receipt / statement / invoice_receipt whenever `findMatchingFileInFolderTree` (`Code.js:2911-2928` — type-blind, matches vendor and period anywhere in the name, recursing into every subfolder) finds any hit. On 2026-07-23 Inbal Peer's genuine tax invoice `InvoiceReceipt_70022.pdf` was flagged *"possible duplicate: 'Inbal Peer July 2026.pdf' already exists for same vendor/period"* and never filed. Confirmed still missing from the finance folders on 2026-08-04 by two independent Drive queries. The durable stamps could not have caught this — `buildIdentityKey` (`Code.js:3146-3157`) hashes vendor|currency|amount|documentNumber|period, and 90022 ≠ 70022. The name check was the sole blocker. August will break identically.
>
> **Erez's intended behaviour**, decided 2026-07-02 and never implemented (it was recorded only inside GEN-338, later closed *Wont Do* for unrelated reasons, so it vanished with the ticket): a payment request files to the To Pay folder, its filename says "payment request", and it stays there permanently; the later tax invoice files normally into the main month folder beside it — no move, no replace.
>
> **The fix.**
> 1\. Both reader prompts learn a fifth document type, `payment_request`, anchored on the document's own self-title (Proforma invoice / חשבון עסקה / דרישת תשלום / payment request / billing note) plus the absence of tax-invoice identity. Explicit guard: a חשבונית מס / Tax Invoice is never `payment_request` even when unpaid; an ordinary unpaid invoice stays `invoice`; if unsure, return `invoice` (mirrors the existing `invoice_receipt` fallback at `Code.js:896`).
>
> 2\. Filename token in the GEN-343 position: `Inbal Peer August 2026 payment request.pdf`. `typeSuffixFor_` (`Code.js:2844`) gains it; `typeSuffixFromName_`'s regex (`Code.js:2879`) gains the two-word alternative so the sheet override-rename path (`Code.js:5013`, `Code.js:5039`) preserves it. `Code.js:2698`'s summary text learns it too, so the summary reads "Filed new payment request" not the raw enum value.
>
> 3\. Filing unchanged, and not unconditional: a payment request normally reads "due" and lands in the To Pay month folder, never moved out. Where it offers only a card/online link and no bank-transfer details, the existing self-pay rule sends it to the main month folder instead (`resolveTargetFolder` is gated on `!meta.selfPay`) — the same folder the later tax invoice uses. Accepted; the duplicate handling below protects it there.
>
> 4\. **The duplicate fix is content-based, not filename-based.** `compareByContent`'s Gemini prompt (`Code.js:2987-2992`) currently asks only `duplicate | different | uncertain` with zero type context — so for a proforma and its own follow-up tax invoice (same vendor, month, amount) the plausible answer is "duplicate", a confidently *wrong* refusal. That prompt is taught the distinction: a payment request / proforma and a tax invoice or receipt for the same vendor and period are DIFFERENT documents even when vendor, amount and month all match; answer "duplicate" only when both are the same kind of document recording the same transaction. Because it reads the documents' own text, this works on legacy, hand-named and Hebrew-named files with no rename and no filename parsing.
>
> 5\. The early check at `Code.js:2622` becomes type-aware from the filename token: it flags only when the matched file's recovered type equals the incoming type; an unreadable type (legacy, untokenised, hand-named) falls through to the better-informed stamp check (`Code.js:2656-2666`), global fingerprint check (`Code.js:2668-2672`) and content comparison. `payment_request` is deliberately NOT added to that check's list — an incoming payment request goes straight to the content comparison, which distinguishes a repeat proforma from one arriving after its tax invoice. Adding it would reintroduce a blind name-based block in the other direction.
>
> 6\. **Order-independent duplicate matching** (Erez, this session: *"The order doesn't matter to me, as long as when I file something manually, I won't have to stick with a certain order."*). `getFilesMatchingBase` (`Code.js:3887`) and `getFilesMatchingBaseInFolderTree` (`Code.js:2893-2909`) both match by `startsWith`, so a hand-named file in any other word order is invisible to duplicate protection. A file-wide grep confirms exactly five call sites, splitting three ways:
> • *Becomes order-independent* — the two candidate sites that have a content comparison behind them: `Code.js:2675` (expenses) and `Code.js:2748` (revenue). Match when the lowercased name contains the vendor AND the period, any order — the same predicate already live at `Code.js:2920`, factored into one shared helper rather than a second copy, preserving the `{name, file, mimeType}` shape `checkForDuplicate` consumes (`Code.js:2930`). `Code.js:2748`'s base carries "revenue" in the middle (`Code.js:2724`); dropping that word is safe as the call is already scoped to the Revenue year folder.
> • *Stays prefix-only* — `Code.js:2794` (`fileEmailBodyReceipt`): it refuses immediately with no content comparison behind it, and none is possible — an email-body doc carries no blob, so `compareByContent` returns `isUncertain` at `Code.js:2985` before reaching Gemini. Widening its net would strictly increase wrong refusals.
> • *Stays prefix-only* — the exact-stem jobs: `Code.js:2867` (type-scoped collision counter) and `Code.js:5057` (override-rename collision guard). Order-independence there would be a regression — a hand-named file would be counted and a correctly-named new file would get a spurious " 2".
>
> 7\. **One-line pre-existing bug folded in rather than deferred:** `checkToPayFolderForMatch`'s `filePeriodRe` (`Code.js:2257`) anchors `Month YYYY` at end-of-string while its caller strips only the extension (`Code.js:2302`), so the period is unparseable on ANY type-suffixed filename — already true for every automation-named file since GEN-343 shipped 2026-07-07. Folded in because step 9's renames would knowingly produce more such names.
>
> 8\. **Sequence:** ship and deploy the code; then recover July's missing tax invoice by re-running the real pipeline on Gmail thread `19f8d61c19b05db0` (verified 2026-08-04: `InvoiceReceipt_70022.pdf` is still attached). This no longer waits on any rename.
>
> 9\. **Then, as bookkeeping only:** survey already-filed payment requests (Hebrew wording and hand-named files included — the earlier Drive survey was not exhaustive, it returned a `nextPageToken`) and rename them to carry the token. Direct Drive rename plus a History-sheet File Name cell update, because `typeSuffixFromName_` returns `''` for an untokenised name so the sheet's own override path cannot ADD a token that isn't there. No longer load-bearing for correctness — the reason to do it is the one Erez raised: an already-filed payment request is mislabelled "invoice".

Step 4 puts a correctness-critical judgement in a Gemini prompt: the failure *direction* is safe (an outage holds for retry at `Code.js:3001`; an unparseable answer returns `isUncertain` at `Code.js:3003`, which flags rather than files), but accuracy is now model-dependent on both the read and compare sides, and Hebrew OCR on scanned חשבון עסקה documents can degrade both. Claude Code never edits your settings file in place — it writes a complete new copy under a temporary name, then swaps it over the original in one move. I confirmed this is what's happening by watching the live file's creation timestamp change on each save, which only happens with a swap. The leftover simply has no owner: nothing sweeps up an abandoned copy on startup.

**Why it only turned up now, and why it will come back.** The backup check looks at every file sitting next to your settings and complains about any name it doesn't recognise — and it matches names *exactly*, with no allowance for patterns. These leftovers are named with a process number and a random string, so every future one has a name nobody can pre-approve. It cannot be silenced by adding this name to the list.
